description: Eleven years without Parliament — ship money, Laudian reforms and rising opposition.
content_html:
Why Did Charles I Rule Without Parliament?

In March 1629, Charles I dissolved Parliament and did not call it again for eleven years. This period is known as the Personal Rule. Charles believed in the divine right of kings — the idea that monarchs were appointed by God and did not need to consult their subjects through Parliament. He had clashed repeatedly with MPs who refused to grant him taxation and who criticised his religious and foreign policies. By governing alone, Charles hoped to avoid those conflicts entirely.

Key Fact

Charles dissolved Parliament in March 1629 and did not call another until April 1640. The period is called the Personal Rule, not the “Eleven Years’ Tyranny” — that label was Whig propaganda used by his opponents.

Financing the Personal Rule: Ship Money

Without Parliament, Charles could not raise taxes by consent. He revived and extended ship money, an old coastal levy, and from 1635 demanded it from inland counties too. Revenue rose dramatically — in 1636 around 90% was collected. Charles argued the Crown could levy ship money without Parliament in times of national danger.

The most famous challenge came from John Hampden, a Buckinghamshire gentleman, who refused to pay twenty shillings in 1637. His trial became a national event. Although Charles won the legal case by seven votes to five, the narrow margin undermined the principle: five judges ruled ship money was unconstitutional. Hampden became a popular hero of parliamentary opposition.

Charles used other prerogative devices to raise money. Distraint of knighthood fined landowners who had failed to be knighted at his coronation — an ancient obligation they had long ignored. Forest laws were revived, fining landowners who had encroached on royal forests. Monopolies were granted to companies in exchange for payments to the Crown. These measures were technically legal but deeply resented as arbitrary impositions.

Laudian Religious Reforms

Charles’s Archbishop of Canterbury, William Laud, introduced a programme of religious reform that alarmed many Protestants. Laud emphasised ceremony, beauty in worship, and the authority of bishops. He moved communion tables to the east end of churches and railed them off, resembling Catholic altars. He ordered clergy to wear vestments and enforced uniformity through the Church courts. Critics accused him of trying to reintroduce Catholicism by the back door.

Laud also used the Court of Star Chamber and the Court of High Commission to silence opponents. William Prynne, Henry Burton and John Bastwick were imprisoned and had their ears cut off in 1637 for publishing pamphlets attacking Laudian practices — an act of brutal censorship that generated public outrage rather than submission.

Key Fact

Laud moved communion tables to the east end of churches and railed them off, used the Star Chamber to silence critics, and enforced the use of vestments. Puritans saw this as a return towards Roman Catholic practice.

The Scottish Crisis and Bishops' Wars

In 1637, Charles and Laud attempted to impose a new Anglican Prayer Book on Scotland. The Scots were strongly Calvinist and regarded the Prayer Book as papist interference. Its introduction sparked a riot in Edinburgh, then widespread resistance. In 1638 Scottish Presbyterians signed the National Covenant, pledging to defend their Kirk against religious innovation.

Charles lacked the army and money to coerce Scotland. Two Bishops’ Wars followed (1639 and 1640), both ending in English humiliation. In the Treaty of Ripon (1640), Charles agreed to pay the Scottish army £850 per day while they occupied northern England. He could no longer govern without parliamentary finance. Necessity, not goodwill, forced him to recall Parliament.

Charles called Parliament in April 1640 (the Short Parliament), but MPs insisted on discussing grievances before granting supply. Charles dissolved it after three weeks. The military crisis deepened, and in November 1640 he was forced to call the Long Parliament. This Parliament immediately attacked Charles’s ministers — Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, was impeached and executed in May 1641. Archbishop Laud was imprisoned, later executed in 1645. Parliament also passed the Triennial Act, requiring Parliament to meet at least once every three years.

The Personal Rule had held together in peacetime only because its financial and religious measures, while unpopular, had not provoked outright rebellion. The Scottish crisis exposed its fatal weakness: without Parliament, Charles lacked the resources to wage war. The period demonstrated that in early modern England, the Crown could not govern effectively without parliamentary cooperation, however much it might wish to.
exam_tip_html: When explaining why the Personal Rule broke down, examiners reward candidates who link financial and religious grievances to the specific Scottish crisis — don’t treat these as separate threads. The ship money case (Hampden 1637), the Prayer Book riot (1637) and the Bishops’ Wars (1639–40) all fall within two years: this clustering shows systemic failure, not random events. In ‘explain why’ and causation questions, identify which factor was most important and why, rather than listing all factors equally.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Charles I governed without Parliament 1629–1640, relying on ship money, distraint of knighthood and other prerogative revenues.
  • Laudian religious reforms alarmed Puritans; the 1637 Prayer Book imposition on Scotland triggered the National Covenant and Bishops’ Wars.
  • Military humiliation and the cost of the Scottish army forced Charles to recall Parliament in 1640, ending the Personal Rule.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of ship money during Charles I's Personal Rule.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: One accurate feature with supporting detail. Example: Ship money was a levy originally charged only on coastal towns but extended by Charles I to inland counties from 1635 to raise revenue without Parliament.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of William Laud's religious reforms in the 1630s.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature with supporting detail. Feature 1: Laud moved communion tables to the east end of churches and railed them off, resembling Catholic altars. Feature 2: Laud used the Court of Star Chamber to silence critics, punishing Prynne, Burton and Bastwick with imprisonment and mutilation in 1637.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I's Personal Rule came to an end by 1640.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-explained causes linked together with clear judgement on which was most significant, e.g. arguing the Scottish crisis was the trigger that exposed the structural weakness of governing without parliamentary finance. Secure: Two causes explained with relevant detail but analysis less developed. Developing: One cause explained or two causes identified but not developed. Emerging: Simple statement with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: John Hampden's ship money trial in 1637 was the most important event of the Personal Rule. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the significance of Hampden's case (constitutional challenge, narrow legal victory, popular impact) against other key events such as the Scottish Prayer Book crisis and Bishops' Wars; reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Argues for and against with relevant evidence across multiple events. Developing: Discusses Hampden with some reference to other events but argument is underdeveloped. Emerging: Mostly descriptive with limited argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Scots opposed Charles I's religious policies in the 1630s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons explained with detail, linked together in a developed argument (e.g. theological Calvinism + fear of episcopal authority + national identity + the specific Prayer Book imposition). Secure: Two well-explained reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One reason explained or two identified without explanation. Emerging: Simple reference to the Scots not liking the Prayer Book.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Personal Rule created financial opposition to Charles I.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains how multiple financial measures (ship money, distraint of knighthood, monopolies, forest fines) individually and collectively generated opposition, linking to constitutional principle. Secure: Two or more measures explained with detail. Developing: One measure described or explanation limited. Emerging: Vague reference to Charles needing money.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year did Charles I first extend ship money to inland counties?
What was the outcome of John Hampden's ship money trial in 1637?
options: Hampden won and ship money was declared illegal
Charles won but only by seven votes to five

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ of 1638 was signed by Scottish Presbyterians pledging to defend their church against religious innovation.
The _____ Parliament met in April 1640 but was dissolved by Charles after just three weeks.
Match each person to their role during the Personal Rule:
right: Refused to pay ship money in 1637
Chief minister executed by Parliament in 1641

flashcard_questions.q: When did Charles I dissolve Parliament to begin the Personal Rule?

flashcard_questions.a: A levy on coastal towns to fund naval defence

flashcard_questions.q: When was ship money extended to inland counties?
What was the result of Hampden's ship money trial (1637)?
flashcard_questions.a: Charles won 7-5 — a narrow victory that undermined the principle

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I?
What specific change did Laud make to church furnishings?
flashcard_questions.a: Moved communion tables east and railed them off
Scottish Presbyterian pledge to defend their church from royal religious interference

flashcard_questions.q: What forced Charles to recall Parliament in 1640?
flashcard_questions.a: The cost of the Bishops' Wars and Scottish army occupation of northern England
Parliament must meet at least once every three years

flashcard_questions.q: Why is 'Eleven Years' Tyranny' not the preferred term for 1629-1640?
flashcard_questions.a: It was partisan Whig propaganda — the correct term is Personal Rule

glossary_terms.definition: King of England, Scotland and Ireland 1625-1649, who governed without Parliament 1629-1640.
The period 1629-1640 when Charles I governed without calling Parliament, relying on prerogative rights and non-parliamentary revenue.
An ancient levy originally charged on coastal towns to fund naval defence, extended by Charles I to inland counties from 1635.
Buckinghamshire gentleman and MP who refused to pay ship money in 1637, taking his case to court as a constitutional test.
Archbishop of Canterbury 1633-1645, whose programme of ceremonial reforms in the Church of England was seen by Puritans as crypto-Catholic.
Earl of Strafford, Charles I's chief minister in Ireland, executed by Parliament in May 1641 for alleged treason.

hero_image_caption: Charles I governed England without Parliament for eleven years from 1629.
